title: 2015: An Annual Report Card on Jack Ma and Alibaba | Top 15 Year-End Stories
excerpt: We should ask more of a giant like this than financial figures
body:
We should ask more of a giant like this than financial figures

Jack Ma was probably not happy to land on the cover of *Forbes* again.

His June 2000 appearance on the international cover of *Forbes* was a landmark piece of early publicity for the e-commerce giant. Fifteen years later, a *Forbes* cover ran with the headline [*Alibaba and Its 40,000 Thieves*](http://finance.qq.com/a/20151127/032292.htm).

![Jack Ma has been on the cover of Forbes twice](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201607021225148MnXPmZihwefoGF2.jpg-w600)

The counterfeit-goods controversy dragged Alibaba into an international lawsuit in 2015 with the luxury group Kering, the parent of Gucci and other brands. When a reporter raised the case, the article says, "he nearly leapt off the sofa." Ma said: "I would rather lose the case, lose money, to win our dignity and respect … How can a Gucci or any other brand handbag be that expensive? It's ridiculous. I know the brand companies are not happy, but I also say this is your business model. You have to rethink your own business model."

Plenty of shoppers may genuinely think Gucci is not worth the price. But for the world's second-largest e-commerce company by market value to answer a counterfeits dispute by attacking the brands' pricing was, to put it mildly, a surprising stance.

That year Ma also pushed back at the lazy assumptions foreign investors made about the Alibaba model:

"E-commerce in the narrow sense is only part of Alibaba Group's strategy today. What we are after is to build an open, transparent, collaborative commercial infrastructure platform … In other words, treating today's e-commerce companies as Alibaba's rivals is like comparing an apple to an apple tree — unfair to both sides."

The letter to shareholders went out in September, when the stock had sunk to a record low, which made it at least a fairly brave move. In 2015, Alibaba had a harder time than anyone imagined — with consumers, investors, regulators, rivals, and itself.

Pulling off the largest IPO in history in 2014 may have fed some "fantasies of fame." Alibaba already looked like an internet company with global reach, yet its outline stayed blurry, weighed down by doubts: an autocratic management style, results that looked too good to be true, the original sin of counterfeit goods, a slowing Chinese economy.

We want to lay out five areas where this company may be less untroubled than people imagine, or than the surface suggests.

### Wealth: The Market Cap Shrank, but Ant Group Is Still Worth Over $40 Billion

Alibaba remains one of China's richest companies, with a market value near 180 billion yuan. Its most recent quarterly report, released at the end of October 2015, showed cash and equivalents above 100 billion yuan — more than Baidu, the old benchmark for strong cash flow.

Behind the strong numbers sit some legitimate accounting moves — for instance, booking the rise in value of majority-held units such as Alibaba Pictures and Alibaba Health into group profit. And when revenue growth fell to a record low in the second quarter of 2015, Wall Street punished the stock without mercy.

![](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702122514GKeNn7lz6cXLi2Zs.jpg-w600)

One more huge asset tied to Alibaba is too big to ignore: Ant Group. In 2015 this internet-finance group, which grew out of Alipay, closed its first public funding round; at the time Bloomberg already valued it above $40 billion.

In early 2016 Ant Group confirmed it was raising a second round, no smaller than the first round's 10 billion yuan. That would likely push it past Uber to become the most valuable unlisted company in the world.

Based on Ma's stakes in both groups, Bloomberg's [Billionaires Index](http://www.bloomberg.com/billionaires/2016-01-18/aaa/aaaga) now ranks him the 22nd richest person in the world, with a personal fortune of $27.5 billion — in China, behind only Wang Jianlin's $30.7 billion.

![The ten richest people in China, per the Bloomberg Billionaires Index](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702122514SxziFK1MXHvQVwNu.jpg-w600)

Across 2015, Alibaba made at least 47 outside investments. The biggest included the $4.5 billion all-cash purchase of Youku Tudou, a 28.3 billion yuan mutual investment with Suning, and a $1.25 billion stake in Ele.me at year's end.

A BNP Paribas analyst report said Alibaba might spend another $38 billion on outside investments in 2016. Whether through buybacks, holding stakes in listed companies, or cashing out, these investments could one day turn into part of Alibaba's own wealth.

### Industry Clout: E-Commerce Is Still the Core

At Singles' Day 2015, after sales passed 80 billion yuan, Ma met the press as usual and gave a short speech. He said Singles' Day had long since stopped being Tmall's game alone; it had become a larger-scale social experiment:

The transaction volume Singles' Day generates today will become the everyday consumption level of all Chinese society ten years from now. Tmall is simply testing whether every link in the chain — merchants, customer service, payments, technology, logistics — is ready for that scale.

![The Tmall Singles' Day gala held at the Water Cube in 2015](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201607021225150N1A5ljeqcPJGhRM.jpg-w600)

This resembles the ambition of Walmart at its peak: using the force of a single brand or platform to shape how an entire country consumes.

But Walmart's influence was never confined to the US market. Its hunt for value-for-money goods eventually marshaled raw materials and products from around the world. Alibaba, by contrast, has declared the goal of "helping ten million small and medium-sized merchants worldwide" do business — yet its core business is still the Chinese market.

On internationalization, what Alibaba can actually do right now is help Chinese consumers buy more foreign goods.

Since 2014, Tmall has been building a cross-border unit called Tmall Global and pouring almost every top international brand into it — a resource edge well ahead of traditional rivals like JD.com and Amazon, and of startups like Xiaohongshu and Yangkeduo. But in the first nine hours of Singles' Day 2015, that unit booked only 1 billion yuan in sales. Given the upfront advertising, the resources poured in, and the rule letting pre-sale orders be paid at midnight, that figure was poor.

How much the Chinese market matters to Alibaba also shows in the new kinds of demand it has had to build up over the past few years.

Take the platforms that connect offline services. When Alibaba invested in Ele.me, it seemed to admit it had been a step slow on O2O. Kuaidi's absorption by Didi in early 2015, the merger of Meituan and Dianping followed by a Tencent investment, and Koubei's wavering direction — none of this was good news for Alibaba.

Logistics, broadly defined, belongs in this O2O discussion too. Alibaba's Cainiao network is copying platform-based operations into the logistics industry, serving courier companies large and small. But judging by this year's Singles' Day, Cainiao's model still cannot fully crack the "last three kilometers" — at least next to the efficient, self-operated logistics that JD.com and Amazon have built.

![During Singles' Day, Tmall used delivery capacity from Suning as a supplement](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702122516FEVibNDW4my0gJ7z.jpg-w600)

The saving grace is that in music, video, sports streaming, and media content, logistics is not the bottleneck. According to the annual group strategy CEO Zhang Yong recently disclosed, virtual goods and services — a bigger segment with relatively higher margins — will be Alibaba's main push in 2016.

### Control: Three Big Businesses Snatched by Tencent, and Three Bets They Both Made

In counting Alibaba's wealth we already noted its 47 outside investments in 2015. But by sheer number and momentum, Tencent looks like the year's winner — it closed 70 investments in 2015 and turned up in three of the biggest M&A deals of the year.

Alibaba had its glory moments too, of course — pulling Suning onto its side, or the $4.5 billion all-cash purchase of Youku Tudou. This was not far from its 2014 thinking: mostly strategic investments, in the hope that the companies it backed would quickly create synergies with its e-commerce core.

Many of Alibaba's investments circled areas where it had already laid foundations — e-commerce, payments, logistics. Tencent, by contrast, was reaching out from its social and gaming base into areas where it had been weaker, such as e-commerce, healthcare, and the local-services and O2O businesses that grow out of social.

Among the startups both companies had spotted and put money into years earlier, several became 2015's classic M&A stories in China's internet industry. The closest to home was the merger of Meilishuo and Mogujie, announced in early 2016.

The companies that finally merged in 2015 — Didi and Kuaidi, Meituan and Dianping, 58.com and Ganji — all carried long histories of investment from both Alibaba and Tencent. But after the mergers, the follow-on money came almost entirely from Tencent. A more dominant Didi and a more independent Meituan further weakened Alibaba's sway over these new giants.

![Among the Asian companies in The Wall Street Journal's "[Billion Dollar Club](http://graphics.wsj.com/billion-dollar-club/)," both Didi and Meituan-Dianping (China Internet Plus) appear](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702122516fA8oDqP9CcsbxS15.jpg-w600)

It is worth looking at what Tencent and Alibaba each did on the other's turf.

In social, Tencent's home ground, Alibaba this year switched its support to the enterprise app DingTalk. In media, it built out stakes in SMG, the *South China Morning Post*, and other legacy outlets. In gaming, its early American bet, Ouya, finally folded, but in 2016 it renamed "UC Jiuyou" to "Alibaba Games."

In e-commerce, Alibaba's home ground, Tencent not only deepened its marketing tie-up with JD.com but also put more money into Meilishuo and Mogujie, two platforms grown out of the Taobao ecosystem. In mobile payments, where the stakes loom even larger, WeChat Pay's reach has crept ever closer to Alipay's.

In both companies' plans, entertainment and offline services are the businesses that will draw more money in the future. Their joint investments in Huayi Brothers, Whaley TV, and Lyft, and their separate investments in Ele.me, all point that way.

### Future Strategy: Building a Second Alibaba on Ant Group

In internet finance, Ant Group has no serious rival.

WeChat Pay's offline reach is now roughly on par with Alipay's. But none of the finance arms of Tencent, JD.com, or Baidu, nor the online operations of traditional banks, can run payments, microloans, wealth-management tools, social credit scoring, and online banking all at once and run them all well, with 400 million users behind them.

![Business units and services under Ant Group](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702122516201hZupdDG4g87KN.jpg-w600)

In a conversation with Qin Shuo about Alibaba's development strategy, Ma laid out a "conveyor-belt strategy": "No internet company can hold an advantage for three to five years straight. So we build a tiered formation, an organic operation … Alibaba's B2B needed repair, so Taobao took the front line, then Tmall, then Alipay came up, then two years later cloud computing, then Cainiao."

From B2B to Taobao and Tmall, then to the Alipay-grown Ant Group, this is Alibaba's bid to widen its reach until every consumption- and transaction-related business sits under its roof. Ant Group — still remaking traditional finance, still on the way up — is the piece Ma has set in place to build a second Alibaba.

Of course, to the US investors who actually set Alibaba's stock price, however bright Ant Group's future looks, it counts for little. So the moment that drew the warmest investor response in 2015 was when Alibaba announced the figures on the share of shopping done on phones.

Two years earlier, Alibaba had declared an "All in Wireless" strategy and committed to the shift to mobile shopping. Today, more than 70% of users would rather shop on Taobao and Tmall by phone than pick through items on a computer screen.

![The trend in "monetization rate," a measure of advertising conversion: orange is mobile, grey is desktop, blue is the overall picture](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702122517PbqN2MzADkyuLh5g.jpg-w600)

Finally, and perhaps a little surprisingly, Alibaba really is pushing into rural areas. According to data Zhang Yong released recently, more than 10,000 Rural Taobao service stations have been set up across China. For these regions, where the network infrastructure is still thin, the lift to consumer appetite has been clear.

You could also read this as a hedge: when the economy is weak, urban shoppers cannot be counted on to keep spending far more every year.

### The Company's — and Its Founder's — Image Has Hardly Changed

In 2015, Jack Ma and Alibaba's management spent a lot of energy at investor conferences, international events, and public letters fit to print, explaining a set of questions to the outside world:

Alibaba is not an e-commerce website but an ecosystem — even the infrastructure for the whole commercial society to come. China's consumer dividend has not run out; the fastest growth is still ahead. We hold Walmart and Amazon in awe, but we will pass them soon.

Yet [the sensational *Barron's* cover story](http://www.barrons.com/articles/alibaba-why-it-could-fall-50-further-1442036618) showed that earnings growth and business models are never the outside world's only test of a company. Judgment is shaped by feeling.

Investors may still recall the "Alipay incident" — the clash between Ma and the board that broke out a few years back, just after Alibaba's B2B business had delisted in Hong Kong and the company was planning its overall listing. Ma later explained that carving out Alipay to secure a payment license was the "imperfect but only correct" choice at the time.

That decision still has two effects today: Alibaba's shareholders cannot share in Ant Group's growth dividend; and it is the partners, not the board, who hold real control of the company, with the constant chance that they may "cross the line" again.

Also raised from time to time is the "original sin" of selling counterfeit goods. On this front, 2015 brought Alibaba a white paper from the State Administration for Industry and Commerce, a class-action lawsuit in the US market, and accusations from several overseas brand associations and groups.

Yet on another stage, built in Wuzhen, Ma said [he welcomes regulation](http://www.17wh.com/kjk/20151219/726296.html), welcomes regulation for all Chinese internet companies:

"Overseas, many people ask whether China's internet is regulated too tightly. But I take this view: whatever the case, this country has managed to produce 700 million internet users, has produced BAT, has produced countless innovations. There is still much here worth learning from and reflecting on."

The remark drew skepticism even from [a staffer at the Ministry of Commerce, where Ma had once worked](http://www.admin5.com/article/20151223/639088.shtml):

"The relevant authorities tried more than once to draw up e-commerce rules and never won enough support; many people feared regulating this young thing to death. And Ma, on one hand, calls for regulating the internet, while on the other calls for open markets — having it both ways. Is that the inner logic of Ma's applause for regulation?"

Why should we watch Alibaba, or any other company of huge scale, with some wariness? A passage from 《Corporation Nation》 roughly explains it:

"Inside the United States, the moves of large corporations directly shape the making of government public policy and the lifestyles and living standards of most people; in other countries, large corporations can sever trade ties with a single nation with ease, or, by direct and indirect means, smile as they drive already cash-strapped foreign governments deeper into debt."

An ever-expanding Alibaba has become an unavoidable part of China's consumer market, yet in 2015 it did not win enough respect in the commercial world to match. What it should be thinking about is this: how to use its influence to pass on more of the spirit of commercial civilization, and to take on more obligations.

That, too, is where the global market holds large companies to a stricter standard.
